But it's not a question of bloody faces. It's a question of what Oric knew, who the guards were under, and whether or not he took necessary and reasonable measures. It was suggested that any soldiers who were seen at the SUP mistreating soldiers were under Oric, and we pointed out that the Trial Chamber found that 20 to 30 fighters from Potocari were under Oric's control. So where's the evidence that any of those soldiers of the SUP were one of those 20 to 30 people from Potocari and that it simply conflicts with the Chamber's own findings. And as far as Kukic is concerned, it's footnote 1500 in the judgement, where the Trial Chamber said, Well, in any event, even if he didn't know from seeing detainees, he knew of the killing of Kukic. Well, there the Trial Chamber conflated two things. The evidence is that Oric knew of Kukic having a heart attack, and separately that he knew or suspected that Halilovic had killed someone. The Chamber conflated those two separate issues. I turn briefly to the submissions of my learned friend Mr. Rogers. He was portraying our position as the War Presidency commanding the military police, but it's more a nuance than that. As we've always said, it's that the military police under Halilovic and the civilian police under Jusufovic were both under the umbrella of the SJB, which was in turn under the War Presidency. That exact command hierarchy is even in -- is in P84 which is one of their most trusted exhibits. It was suggested that Djilovic was disbelieved by the Trial Chamber for various reasons. Well, the Trial Chamber didn't give any of those reasons in the judgement. It didn't say, We find Djilovic uncredit-worthy because she made a mistake about Halilovic or because she wasn't at all meetings. That's part of the problem of this judgement, there are no clear credibility findings. In any event, in terms of the mistake about Halilovic, in fact, it reflects, does it not, that he was at the War Presidency so often that she assumed he was a member of the War Presidency. She was the technical secretary to the War Presidency, so she was very much absolutely in a position to know what was happening there; it was her duty. Sacirovic was not some outsider. He was on the same floor, practically next to the office of the president of the War Presidency. As far as the references to -- I'll take that as an indication that I have two minutes remaining and nothing else. The references to the transcript we can disagree and go back and forth between Mr. Rogers and myself about what was actually said and what was not said, and I think really the only suggestion we can make is that obviously the Chamber review those transcripts carefully and it will be seen what was said. But D247, yes, it's 28th of February, 1994, but they're adopting the report for the whole prior year, and Meholjic testified to that at T6999. There are many points I would like to make about the exhibits, the Prosecution exhibits. We've dealt with them, I think, fully in our appeals filing; and given I only have a minute or two left, I would just like to say again Krnojelac -- well, actually, my learned friend Ms. Jarvis referred to layering and that layering can show as part of being a commander. But we're not complaining of vertical layering; it's a vertical layering and then horizontal, horizontal, horizontal, horizontal. 7(3) vertically, but then aiding and abetting by omission, aiding and abetting. That's the horizontal layering which we say is a daisy chain. And, finally, prison camp cases are fundamentally different from this case. Krnojelac was a prison warden in an institution, a prison. No command hierarchy has been shown over this prison. It's never been pleaded or much less proved that Oric was anything resembling a prison warden, and that too is totally new. Thank you, unless I can assist you further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There are no additional questions. This concludes the submissions of the parties on appeal. A judgement will be rendered in due course. And, Mr. Jones, at that time, you will see who can interpret my signal for the two minutes as a sign of victory, but it's on truth and not on winning a case. I want to thank the parties for their submissions and all their efforts to direct us to the transcripts and the judgement in a very precise way, both orally and in writing. I want to thank everybody having prepared this hearing and having assisted us during the entire hearing. In particular, gratitude goes to the interpreters who had during the last two days some hard times, but we, only with their assistance, were able to follow the proceedings and as it was also translated into B/C/S and into French. Thank you for this huge effort. The appeals hearing stands adjourned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.25 a.m.
